utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the absence of Judge Mindua, we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Tapuskovic, you're to continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamenov, good morning.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You'll remember that yesterday we began the examination-in-chief and that the report that you had compiled was assigned a number for identification. That is being loaded into the electronic system. My first question would be and -- would be to kindly ask, explain to the Judges, in what way you carried out this examination of the incidents and how you analysed them as presented in your report.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out this analysis on the basis of the available documents that the Prosecutor's Office had submitted and disclosed to the Defence. Having studied the available documents, I presented my conclusions, as you can see in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From all these documents that you have analysed, which particular documents were the main foundation for your conclusions and which you could not have avoided in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic documents that I used and that were the crucial ones were the documents compiled by the police and the medical records containing information about the victims, the site of the incident, and the type of the injuries sustained. The major problem that I faced was the lack of medical records and I also mentioned that in the conclusions of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever try to analyse anything relating to witness statements or did you believe that that was beyond the scope of your remit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried and I did analyse the witness statements. I also tried to carry out an analysis thereof. However, due to contradictory witness statements between their statements, because some of the witnesses gave one, two, or even three statements, their evidence does not correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After you had reached this conclusion, did you think that this was something that should have been done by someone else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that it was not my job to determine which statement was accurate and true. I believe that this is the -- under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal and therefore I didn't deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to complete this examination within a specified time limit, Mr. Stamenov. We will not be able to repeat everything that you wrote down in your report, and this is largely going to be the subject of the

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: number of questions that could be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and that perhaps have not been fully explained in your report. One of these issues, very specific issues, that may be of relevance is the weapons that you mentioned as the ones that could possibly have been used in the conflict and which are depicted in your report. Can you tell us what kind of weapons, among the ones mentioned, was not at the disposal of the Yugoslav army and of which you are not able to confirm whether it was in the possession of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I had, and still have, the Yugoslav People's Army did not have a 7.62-millimetre Dragunov rifle, sniper rifle, because this particular weapon was still in the process of development. As for the information whether this weapon was at the disposal of the VRS, I have no such information. And I know that the factory in Kragujevac called Zastava had not started the production of this particular weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the origin of this Dragunov rifle? Which army did it have?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made in Russia, or rather, in the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you tell us now because it's been discussed widely something about 7.9 bullet? What kind of infantry weapons are used - interpreter's correction - what weapons use these bullets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7.9-millimetre bullets can be used by light machine-guns; machine-guns; M-53, 7.9 millimetres; and a semi-automatic rifle, M-76, 7.9 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 of the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, can we please have the document MFI-360, and that's DD00-4689, be brought up. And if we can go to page 5 in the B/C/S version and also page 5 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Well, actually, in order for me to be able to ask you the question that I want to ask you, we have to turn to the next page in both versions. In these pictures numbered 3 to 8, what do they depict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs numbered 3 to 8 depict the view through the sight, through the optical sight of a sniper rifle M-76. One can see the view of a person's figure at the distance ranging between 100 and 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. This first picture shows, on page 5, shows us what distance?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first picture on page 5 shows the view of a human figure as seen from the distance of 100 metres. The hand or the arm has number 1, and each subsequent photograph, this person that was within the field of view is holding a cardboard with a number which indicates the distance.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. In order not to go through all these photographs, can we now look at the last one on page -- I'm sorry. Actually, page 8 in the B/C/S version. That's photograph number 7 or 8. Doesn't matter. Let's look at photograph 8. What does it show? What is the range, and if you can explain us further?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 7 shows the view of a human figure at the distance of 500 metres, and photograph 8 shows the same view, only from the distance of 600 metres. However, in photograph number 8, the figure is already in the shadow and therefore it cannot be easily discernible.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If we look at photograph number 7 and all the previous photographs, what would be the optimum conditions in which these photographs were made?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs were made under nearly ideal weather conditions. It was sunny and the visibility was excellent. The view through the optical sight is real and there is no magnification. The camera was placed in the position of the eye looking through the optical sight, and these were real photographs corresponding to what a person actually can see if looking through an optical sight.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain to the Judges why you made these photographs. First of all, tell me, did you take them yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it along with my assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you do that in relation to these distances and then you stopped at the range of 600 metres? Why was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular situation, what I wanted to do was to show, in practical terms, how a marksman sees a human figure through an optical sight and that in the ranges in excess of 600 metres, given that an optical sight can provide a quadruple magnification, it is already difficult to spot the target of the size of a human figure. In excess of 600 metres, it is difficult to see and it is difficult to select this particular target.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If you had had an opportunity to make these kind of photographs from a particular location - I won't mention any specific location relating to this case - and if we assume that this was the place from which a shot came, would you have been able to say that it was possible at all to fire at any specific target?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had an exact place been determined from which a shot was fired, an optical sight could have been placed there and we could then try and simulate that situation by placing a person at the very spot. Given such conditions, one would have been able to see the appearance of such a human figure as viewed through an optical sight and we would have been able to check whether fire could have been opened from that location. In any case, had I been given an opportunity, I would have done that in order to verify the assertions in place as to whether there was a possibility to open fire from that location.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I have to ask you the following: Did you give any thought to do that, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contemplated the idea. I put that idea forth to the Defence; however, the response I was given was that it cannot be done for several reasons. Therefore, I gave up on the idea and I submitted these photographs instead just to illustrate that such an exercise can actually be carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I'd like to be more specific since, for example, you know that what is mentioned here is inter alia as the place from which sniper fire was opened was the marketplace, and that is specifically mentioned in the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic. The location referred to there is Spicaste Stijena, or Sharpstone. Had you been able to go to the very ridge of what in this case is called Spicaste Stijena, would that have been of any use in order to make photographs of this nature in order to try and shed some light on one or several of the incidents you had the opportunity to analyse?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From that location one could make similar photographs, similar to these, on which we would be able to see what and at what distance can be seen through this type of sight belonging to a sniper rifle. As I said, the magnification is quadruple. In any case, had there been a possibility, I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: It seems to me that in your report you don't deal -- well, this is the optical sight. What other sights are there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sniper rifle can be equipped with two other types of sights. The basic one is the mechanical one. There is also the possibility to mount a passive night-sight which is not in the regular combat kit that goes with this rifle. I apologise, I forgot to turn my mobile off. I apologise to the Court. I forgot to turn it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's finally off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finally managed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Do I need to remind you of the question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, this sniper rifle has two additional sights, the mechanical one as the basic type, and the passive or night-sight as an additional sight that can be used.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Speaking of those sights, they are not the same as this optical sight. I'm asking you all this because I'd like you to explain to the Chamber, or perhaps if you can sketch that for us, to show us what the situation looked like. That would be of some importance, I believe. What is the situation when one uses only the mechanical sight? Can you sketch that for us briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the gist of your question. The mechanical sight can be used only once the optical sight is removed from the mount. As for using the mechanical sight to aim, it is somewhat different compared to the optical sight. And yes, I can draw a sketch for you.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Please do and then provide us with a brief explanation. I think you can do this exercise quickly.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mechanical sight consists of two elements, the cross-hairs and the rear part of the sight. This is the view from the marksman's position. If we are trying to fire from such a weapon at an aim which is 100 metres away, and if it is a human figure, its width is approximately 50 to 60 centimetres. At a distance of 100 metres, this is more or less what it looks like. This is the view of the human figure and the position of the cross-hairs and the rear. At the distance of 200 metres, the view is like this. At 300 metres, this is the view. 400 metres, something like this. This is a comparison of a view of the human figure. Something similar would go for the optical sight, but this would depict the use of a mechanical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to have this admitted as a Defence exhibit. I will seek some further clarification, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If we keep increasing the distance, since you stopped here, but if we go on to 4, 5, 600 metres, I believe the reduction would be correspondent to the ones shown here, reduction in size, that is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The larger the distance, the target is smaller.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And by using the mechanical sight, what would be the ability of that marksman to hit the target in terms of direct fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this type of mechanical sight, which can be mounted on both the sniper rifle and the automatic rifle and the light machine-gun, that is, all of the types of weapons mentioned in the incidents, well, with such a sight, anything beyond 200 metres is difficult. As you can see, as of 200 metres, it is very difficult to line up the rear and the front sight and the target is far smaller than the front part of the sight. With that mechanical sight, one can aim successfully between 50 and 100 metres. The rest is quite imprecise.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You described to us the ideal conditions - good visibility, plenty of sunlight - but regardless of whether we use the optical or the mechanical sight, what impact do such conditions have on aiming, irrespective of distance?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weather conditions do have an impact when aiming with an optical and a mechanical sight. That impact is the same as would be with a regular observer. If there is fog and low visibility, we cannot see things well with the naked eye. The same goes for any type of aiming. It is far more difficult in such conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Well, let us leave fog aside or such extreme conditions which make any aiming impossible. But if there are heavy clouds, to what extent does it hinder the precise system of shooting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Heavy clouds, well, I don't know exactly what you mean by "heavy clouds," but in any case it reduces visibility and it certainly makes any observation more difficult, the viewing of the target, and hence the aiming is more difficult as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: As regards any of the incidents mentioned, and I think there are 12, did you have any data on some of those incidents as to the visibility on that day when they took place? Did you have such precise information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received some information from the NATO command that was in charge of the Butmir airport and the Sarajevo airport. I had reports concerning five out of 12 incidents. These are the incidents: Number 1, it was rainy and foggy. The incident number 14, rain in the morning and poor visibility. The incident number 2, before 9.00 poor visibility; later on, cloudy. The incident number - excuse me - 18, poor visibility and cloudy. And according to a witness statement in the case of the incident number 10, visibility was poor and there was fog; however, that is not NATO information. As for the other incidents, I had no reports.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you DD00-4389. It is a NATO report for the 16th of January of 2007 relating to the autumn of 1994. When drafting the report, did you have this NATO report before you, since it pertained to the situation as it was at the airport at the time? They drafted that for their own purposes and now we have it at our disposal. Did you take that report into account as well as its contents concerning the dates you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the cover page of the document before me. The data contained follows and I consulted it when drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document, DD00-4389, would be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the mechanism of ricochet? You mentioned that at page 20 in the B/C/S. In the English I think it is page 11.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned the term of ricochet briefly. A definition is given. I wanted to say that a projectile that has ricochetted receives an undefined trajectory which cannot be determined in any way, it cannot be foreseen, since such a projectile, depending on the type of surface it hit, can even go back in a straight line. What is particularly interesting is that such a projectile does not have a defined ballistic trajectory that could be analysed. Such a projectile is undefined in terms of trajectory. It can also contain only parts of projectile. And it is very difficult to establish the line of fire viewed from the position of the victim.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is telling me that the interpretation is incorrect, and it's very important. Maybe my colleague can explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A moment ago the expert used an expression for the bullet which ricochetted, and in B/C/S the word was "tumbati." In fact, those are two words, "tumba," from the verb "tumbati," which has an impact on the determination of the trajectory of the bullet. Therefore, I'd like to ask that we correct the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you saying it should be? It's not clear to me exactly what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the expert used a term for the bullet ricochetting, an expression in B/C/S. I myself do not know what the English word is. This is on page 11, line 11. And this is a word that's missing in the interpretation and it's an important term. He said the bullet, and the verb in B/C/S is "tumba." I don't know what the exact word is in English, and I myself do not know what this term is but it's very important. My colleague has just said that what this means is that basically after the ricochet, the bullet bounces and spins, it spins. And if you were to describe the movement, that's what it is. It's a spinning movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's the idea of the spinning movement that is missing in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The closest translation would be rolling over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The closest translation would be rolling over or turning over, tumbling. Tumbling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tumbling. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: While we're still dealing with your report, I would like to ask you a general question that you mentioned at the very end of your report relating to the analysis of the activities - that's page 22 in B/C/S and page 13 in the English version - where you say a few things about this issue. Could you please explain to the Judges: Is it possible at all in an urban environment and on the basis of a shot fired from an infantry weapon to determine the origin of fire or the direction from which the shot came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an urban environment it is extremely difficult to establish the direction from which a shot was fired based on the sound that the shot produces, for the simple reason that in an urban environment there is multiple deflection of the sound and it bounces against the walls of the buildings. Therefore, one has a feeling that one has heard the sound coming from the right-hand side where in actual fact the shot was fired from a completely different location. Therefore, it is extremely difficult based on the sound to determine the direction from which a shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were preparing your report, you also studied an expert report who provided his opinion for the Prosecution. I'm talking about Mr. Van der Weijden. What you said just now in this context and in response to my question is the same thing contained in Mr. Van der Weijden's report in relation to any of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have studied Mr. Van der Weijden's report, and in one of the incidents he offered a conclusion saying that probably due to the urban environment and the bouncing off, it was very difficult to determine the location from which fire was opened. I don't remember exactly which number this incident has, but I do remember that this gentleman mentioned this in his report and I fully agree with him.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question relating to these general matters and it is not directly related to your report. You have described sniping activities and on the previous page you spoke in general terms about how snipers operate. What I'm interested to hear from you is, does every army - let us now disregard the warring parties here - does every army have a sniper squad? That is to say, that every army, I presume, has a sniping squad equipped with rifles.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if every army has a sniper squad. Sniper squads do not exist as such. It depends on the formation of the army where snipers are going to be positioned and they have different names. Sometimes it's a sniper; sometimes there are pairs of snipers. And it depends on the establishment of the army in question. Therefore, snipers and sniper rifles exist in every army; only it depends how they deploy them and that depends on the structure of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this - and I will show in the course of the day the relevance of my question - is it customary for all armies in the world to make preparations and training, as they do for all other kinds of weaponry, and that that should also include the training of snipers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a common practice because members of the army are being trained for every kind of weapons that they are using, including sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And under what circumstances are snipers being used? I'm talking about a regular situation, but I'm also talking about the situations where there are certain combat activities. You did explain this to a certain extent in your report, but I would like to hear it from you anyway.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I explained the notion of a sniper, the origin of it, and what it entails, what kind of assignments a sniper carries out.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to dwell on this any longer. The time is passing by very quickly. I have a few more important issues to discuss with you. In response to one of the questions posed by Mr. Docherty when he examined Mr. Van der Weijden - and that's on page 4328 of the transcript, lines 14 to 18 - what is the role or the significance of medical records in determining the origin of fire? In response to that question, Mr. Van der Weijden said: "If it is possible to establish the entry and exit wound on the victim and the exact position of the victim, it is possible to determine where the shot came from." What is your position on this? You already mentioned something in this context, but what is your position regarding this? What is the usefulness in addition to the position of the body of the victim, and what is the significance of medical records in order to provide a highly likely determination of the origin of fire in specific terms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with this statement of Mr. Van der Weijden because that is the basis for establishing the origin and direction of fire. I also stated these three elements in my report as well and I particularly emphasised the importance of medical records as one of the crucial links in the whole process of determining the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Speaking of ballistics, and if we are going to use medical jargon, are there any specific terms that describe the direction? How do you call these wounds that are found on victims and which can serve as a benchmark for determining the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can have a gunshot and an entry and exit wound on the victim, and the path through which the bullet passes is called the tunnel or the canal and it is extremely important for determining the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: With regard to the 12 incidents that you had an opportunity to study, how many incidents did you have this particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 12 incidents that I studied and analysed, only in one incident did I have this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Please, please, at this point can you tell me just the number of the incident that you're referring to, because we are going to have to deal with a number of other incidents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution earlier made a written submission objecting to the witness testifying about these matters of death investigation and I want to renew for the record our objection to these questions and answers which, in the Prosecution's submission, are beyond the colonel's expertise. He is not a physician; he is not trained in death investigations. His expertise is in shooting and in weaponry. And therefore, we renew at this time the objection previously made in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your response, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My response is that is absolutely identical, what Mr. Docherty said. I'm not going to ask the witness to go into any analysis relating to this issue. This is something that perhaps will be addressed by a medical expert. All I wanted to hear from him, in how many incidents that he had analysed was this specific piece of information provided that could be of assistance in dealing with this matter. Very quickly, I'm going to ask him in a proper manner about these issues totally irrespective and regardless of the medical records. My intention solely was to hear that, out of the total of 12 incidents, only in one instance was this autopsy report provided showing that -- what kind of wound was involved and what kind of direction was involved, and nothing beyond that. The witness says that this was the case in only one incident.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And the number of the incident is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's incident number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Incident number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, the Chamber does not take the view that the witness is being asked, or will be asked, about medical matters beyond his expertise. We'll allow the question and we'll monitor -- we'll monitor it very carefully, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to get that one single answer from the witness corresponding to what was the number of the incident which had to do with an entry/exit wound.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you just tell me where that incident occurred, and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in the incident number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you something that had to do with Mr. Van der Weijden as well concerning the place, the position, and medical reports. If there's any of those missing and if there were factors that could not have been established beyond any reasonable doubt, what is the only thing that one can conclude?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the projectile trajectory fired from a certain weapon is not concluded once it impacts the victim but rather it extends through the victim by causing a degree of destruction, in order for us to establish the direction of fire, it is of crucial importance to know the exact spot where the victim was at the moment when he or she got hit. The victim's position is crucial, as is the canal I mentioned, with an entry or an entry/exit wound, since it is an extension of the trajectory. Without that, one cannot determine the line of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned something and that is why I was asking you all these questions, since all that is already described in your report. But at page 19 in the B/C/S, which is page 10 and 11 in the English, you mentioned there the trajectory. Could we go to that page first, please, and I'd like to see the drawing you had made. I will ask you to sketch something for us again. But before that, could you please explain to us the existing trajectory. What does that curve represent?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: A projectile fired from any type of weapon in any given direction does not move horizontally and in a straight line. It moves along a certain ballistic curve. Its shape and size depend on the distance at which that projectile was fired. The further the target, the more horizontal the curve.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The further the target, the bigger the curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I think there is something with the transcript that we need to correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to this response. On page 19, lines 4 to 8, I think we need to check because the expert stated in B/C/S that the further away the target is, and the transcript says "the further the target and then the more horizontal the curve," that was a quotation. In fact, it was the opposite. It was that the curve is more horizontal if the target is closer, whereas the transcript said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it should be, if I understand you correctly, the nearer the target, the more horizontal the curve? Yes, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank my learned friend and perhaps we should clarify this further, since we are discussing direct firing here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly? Initially the trajectory is horizontal; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial stage of the trajectory is a straight line.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the length of that initial stage in which the line is straight?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not ideally straight in terms of ballistics. But up to, say, 500 metres it is almost straight.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You did not link your sketch and the curve to certain distances in your report on this page. Therefore, could you sketch that for us briefly now.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that, but I would need a pen. I will show you three different distances here. We'll take the maximum distance of 1.200 metres, then another distance of 500 metres, and let's say 300 metres. The trajectory for the distance of 1.200 metres has the initial part of the trajectory and the descending part of the trajectory. Since this is a ballistics curve, the angle of elevation is approximately 10 metres above ground. At the distance of 500 metres, the elevation is between 86 and 90 centimetres. At a distance of 300 metres, the trajectory is almost horizontal. The elevation there is about 26 centimetres. This is what I tried to explain. The shorter the distance, the more horizontal the curve; and the bigger the distance, the bigger the curve.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: How does that impact on precision?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closer the target, the higher probability of hitting it. Of course, I'm discussing a sniper rifle here. This is from the firing tables for a sniper rifle, M-76. That rifle is very successful for the distances up to 500 metres, since an average person is 175 centimetres tall and we have up to 90 centimetres of elevation. Up to some 500 metres, it is more -- it is easier to target such targets. At large distances, the elevation is around 10 metres. Therefore, the probability of hitting such targets is very low.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If we discuss the targeting of such aims at certain distances with a mechanical sight, since you mentioned a figure of 50.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a mechanical sight, well, as regards the projectile ballistics, it is the same for the optical and the mechanical sight. However, it is far more difficult to aim with a mechanical sight, hence the degree of success of hitting the target is lower and it is best at the distances of 50 to 100 metres when talking about a mechanical sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have this admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: A few moments ago I asked you about medical reports. I will not use such documentation since it has no link to your expertise. But given that it was established that an entry and an exit wound can be indicative of the line parallel ... and if that canal corresponds to the line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please phrase his question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreter is asking you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What I said is if - if- there is a situation at hand in which a projectile went through a body by showing or exhibiting a trajectory parallel to the ground, in that case if the height is 120 centimetres, what would have to be the line of fire of the projectile? Could you draw that for us. Perhaps you can draw a person and draw a line through the area where the stomach should be parallel to the ground, and then I will ask additional questions. Since I can see that you can draw pretty well and pretty quickly, I'd like you to do that. Draw a person first and follow up with what I've asked you to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand your question. This is the figure of a person.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There you go. You also said that the wound exhibited a canal parallel to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a while ago that the ballistic trajectory of a bullet fired from a weapon corresponds to a ballistic curve which is not completed at the point of hitting the target but moves on, as shown here. If the height at this point is 1 metre, as you said, from the ground and if it is parallel, therefore, at the point of entry it is also 1 metre, I suppose - I don't know where the bullet came from exactly - if this is the point of entry and the point of exit --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Let us not discuss whether it entered from one side and went out through the other side. But I want to stress the following: If the canal is parallel to the ground, irrespective of where the place of entry was.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case I did not understand your question. I understood that the projectile was fired also from the height of 1 metre. In that case the firing position could be at the height of 1 metre, independently of whether it was through the left or through the right. If a firing position was different, if it was from a building or elsewhere ...

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I don't want to mention any buildings, but let's say the shot was fired from the height of 15 metres. What would be the trajectory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it came from an elevation, let's say this is the position of the marksman, and if this was the height, that trajectory would have been completely different. And as I said, the trajectory goes through the victim and it would exhibit a different angle compared to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Let me hear that again. If the canal was parallel to the ground and if the parallel line drawn on this silhouette and if it was at the height of 1 or 100 -- 1 metre or 1.3 metres, what was the height from which the bullet came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the trajectory, the height would have been the same, independently of what side the bullet came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have this admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like a number of photographs now to be shown and I will try to cover another two topics before I finish my examination. These are the photographs taken from the set of photographs made by the Tribunal, C10, and let's take, for example, photograph number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Could you say that you have studied both this photograph and other documents relating to this incident? Which incident are we talking about here? Is that incident number 2?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely incident number 2 and this is the picture showing the view of the passage between the buildings, or rather, a tunnel under the building.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You are aware of what the indictment says with regard to this incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You also know that it's being claimed that the fire came from the school for the blind and that's the building, the contour or the shape of which you can see in the background of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Would you be able to deny or dispute that there is visibility and that there is a field of vision here with respect to the roof of this building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the spot from which the photograph was taken, it shows that there is certainly visibility, including all the buildings that one can see through this passage. You can see a few buildings; therefore, there is visibility in existence.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In order for me to be able to ask you certain questions, I would like the Prosecution to show us the video which we are not able to show. After we've seen this photograph, I have further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's document P172, which was used in the examination of Witness W-62. And if we can pause the video at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the individual in this video is a protected witness. I would ask that we go into private session. I would also ask that this portion be redacted and that I think we're in time to stop it from being broadcast due to the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Sir, you have seen this video and the photograph as well. You have already confirmed that the roof of the building from which the shot allegedly came from was within the field of vision from the spot where the witness showed the position of the boy who was shot on that day. Would it be of any assistance if you had known what the field of vision looked like from the roof, or approximately from the roof, of the building from which the shot supposedly came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said earlier, it would have been useful to have the view from the position from which it is believed that the shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Would accurate information about the height of the building would also be significant and useful for what you would be able to say about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one of the elements that is necessary for establishing the actual situation, and in this instance it is particularly interesting in terms of the canal of the entry and exit wound on this victim.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If the victim was on the ground as shown by the witness and if fire came from the roof of any of the buildings, including the one mentioned here, and supposing that it has certain sight - correction - height, and I'm not going to go into that, how would that trajectory look like in that case? Would you be able to determine the trajectory in any way, since there is a significant difference in height between the ground and the height of the building from which the shot supposedly came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly the area that one can see through the passage and the position of the victim as shown by the witness indicates that the projectile may have been fired from any building within this field of vision. And for that reason it is very important to have the information about the position of the entry and exit wound, because this is the wound that was inflicted in this particular incident which would serve as a basis, and the angle of the wound could tell us more about the position from which the shot came.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: My question was if the victim was standing on the ground and the person shooting was either on the roof or at an elevation which is 10 or 12 metres above the ground, what trajectory would look like? Would it be horizontal? Would it be -- go from top to bottom, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would go from top to bottom. As I showed in the drawing that I made, this trajectory would go from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I didn't make any reference to any incidents and, in principle, whether this would be useful and purposeful in any incident, we'll go into that later. I'm asking you about this specific incident. Does that mean that the trajectory would be descending from up, down?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Is that why it was necessary, as you mentioned, to know about the entry wound?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I already asked you this and you explained it to me, that a gunshot has an entry wound and an exit wound. If the shot came from above in a descending line, how would this wound canal look like? Would the canal have, in principle, to correspond to the trajectory of the gunshot?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially the canal is an extension of the trajectory of a projectile and it practically shows the direction of the shot. And it is, as I said, an extension of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You didn't have any of these measurements and parameters.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You said that this person could have been shot from any building situated in the direction and with regard to the spot from which the shot was claimed to have come.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: After you've seen this photograph indicating that the person was outside the passage, and approximately, based on the photograph, would you say, was the person hit from the passage? And I'm saying "approximately" because we don't have that measurement either.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried, while the film was going on, to make a comparison between the video and the photograph in which you can see these cobbles or flagstones on the ground, and I presume that they're about 40 centimetres in length. The video shows the passage shot from about, as I was able to calculate from the distance measured, 25 or 30 flagstones, whereas I wasn't able to do that on the video. If we suppose that there are 30 flagstones, the total distance from the passage would be around 12 metres. That's my rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: All these measurements that you have just mentioned and the information about what can be seen from the roof and all other parameters relevant for the distance, would all of this be relevant for establishing the exact path and the trajectory, since there is an assessment made that the distance was about 320 metres? And therefore would one be able to say that this person was -- could have been shot from the roof of this building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very interesting to look at the exact position of the victim, and that is why we are talking about these measurements, how far the victim was from the passage and what position he was in, and that is why these measurements would be useful. As for other measurements, they would be useful in the process of analysis of the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You said 10 to 12 metres. Apart from the possibility for shooting the person from the passage, there is still space outside the passage, in front of this car. Was it possible for this victim to be shot from some different direction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the footage and the photograph, the victim could have been shot from its right-hand side and from its left-hand side. It could have been shot from direction of the building, though, having in mind the body position. It could have been hit -- could not have been hit from the ground floor, from the shop shown there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In such cases would the canal of the entry and exit wound be of any use?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case such a canal of the entry and exit wound is of crucial importance, independently of what the environment is like.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: There are several other photographs concerning the incidents regarding street-cars. These are the incidents 1, 6, 8, 13 and 14. I would like to show you something about that and then I would conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a 65 ter photograph 2825.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the photograph, I wanted to ask you this, since it has something to do with the tram incidents: Is there a rifle bullet with a fragmentation effect? Is there a projectile made in such a way that it would break up into fragments? Have you ever heard of such a projectile?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the weaponry used in these incidents, these being sniping rifles, automatic rifles, and light machine-guns, there is no such bullet which would have the fragmentation effect. We only have the classical bullet; then we have a marker bullet, an armour bullet and incendiary bullet, and this is all for the 7.62-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: When a bullet is being fragmented, is it due to some other circumstances and not because it was envisaged for that bullet to become fragmented?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The classical or universal bullet has the charge and the casing. At the moment of impact, if the surface is hard, the two can separate and then what can occur is fragmentation. But this is not intentional. That is because of the hardness of the surface.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Can you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I mentioned a number of incidents that had to do with street-cars, if I may call them that. These are 1, 6, 8, 13 and 14. Were there any indications that in any of the cases that the street-car in question was stationary when hit?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were all in movement.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Very well. When you look at this photograph, what is characteristic as to the tram lines that can be seen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on the lower part of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: I guess you can see it better now. If you can, and I will conclude shortly, although I have some photographs still to show, but could you tell us something about the lines at the place where they cross the road. Perhaps you can sketch it for us and explain a couple of things to us, then. On a piece of paper, not on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the photograph I can see tram lines. If we look at the right-hand side of the photograph, that's in the direction of Novo Sarajevo moving towards old town and Marin Dvor. This is an intersection, or rather, a place where the line crosses the street in front of the Holiday Inn to the right-hand side of the road towards the school of philosophy, in the direction of Marin Dvor. You asked me about the position of the lines when crossing the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yes. In any of the incidents you studied was the exact place where the street-car was hit established at the moment when people were injured?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the incidents I studied, according to the witness statements which, on several occasions, were actually contradictory --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Do not go into that, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incidents happened between Pofalici and the school of philosophy. That's the stretch. But I never had at my disposal the exact position of any given street-car.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: If we consider an articulated street-car, what would its movement be just before it turns the bend? What would be its position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you mean an articulated street-car when it starts turning. Therefore, it is coming along the straight patch and then turning and it would look something like this.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And once it is in the bend?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll draw that with a dotted line. This would be one portion of the street-car and the other portion would be here, approximately. We can mark this position with an A and this with a B. The position B is the street-car at the moment of entering the bend.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: In that situation certain parts of the tram would be pointing in another direction.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There would be an angle between the front and the rear part of the street-car, depending on the width of the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have this sketch admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show an additional two photographs from the set -- from a set of court documents. The photographs are C14, photograph 22.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: What is discussed is that the street-cars were hit, but can you tell us from what direction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these incidents, the Metalka building is usually mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You have seen all these photographs. You've studied the footage. When a street-car is at this position, can you see the Metalka building from that place at all? Can you see it from the street-car?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows the place where the street-car cuts across the road, and from this position shown on the photograph, one cannot see the Metalka building.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is necessary to admit this yet again, since it is an exhibit already. Could we please see photograph 25 from the same set of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Concerning the Metalka building, what can you tell us about this photograph? What is the relation between the tracks shown here and the Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph shows the place where the tracks move through the middle of the road towards the Holiday Inn. We can see the left and the right side of the street. The tracks are in between, cutting across. The Metalka building is visible from the direction of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to show one last photograph before I conclude. This is from the photographic set C23. Let's have a look at that photograph, although there are others as well, and then I'll have a couple of questions. I apologise, C3, photograph number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: From this place, well, we can see the buildings that are visible on the photograph. If one were on the Metalka roof or at one of the windows, what would that person be able to see here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a panoramic view. I presume it was taken from the Metalka building roof or from the building itself. Through the branches you can see parts of the Zmaja Od Bosne Street and the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You mentioned the branches, hence my last question: Were there any branches in the direction of the three other buildings and the Holiday Inn? Can you see that from the photograph, or perhaps you cannot say?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What branches? In what direction? What buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: The three tall buildings to the right-hand side and we can see the Holiday Inn far in the background.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the direction of Zmaja Od Bosne Street and it goes on further towards Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Thank you. It is a matter of some other assessments. I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you prefer to be addressed as mister or as colonel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. You can address me as sir, as I appear here as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm going to do the following this morning: I'm going to have some questions about your career and your background. I'm going to have some questions then about the methodology that you used in preparing your report. I'll have a few questions about one or two of the specific incidents that Mr. Tapuskovic asked you about. And then I'll conclude by asking you some questions as a military officer about a topic that I know as rules of engagement and then I'll be done. I don't think this will take very long. And if you have any questions or if my question is not clear, please ask me to clarify it because I do want us to communicate well. You are currently a colonel in the Serbian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And before it was the Serbian army, you were an officer in the Yugoslavian People's Army; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How long have you been a military officer? How many years?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in looking through your curriculum vitae, I noted that you have a good deal of experience in competitive shooting and in fact have even judged that at a very high international level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Among the list of your professional accomplishments and qualifications, I did not see that you had ever undergone sniper training. Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this training as part of the curriculum in the secondary military school and at the military academy. That's one of the subjects that is being taught and that is the sniper activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Both the Yugoslavian People's Army and the Serbian army, though, have training for soldiers who are actually going to work as snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you yourself are not a sniper now, nor have you worked as a sniper at any time in your military career; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never a professional sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Nor have you ever been a police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a police officer, but I did provide instruction at the police academy to police officers relating to the use of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you were teaching the police the sort of things that you've been testifying to here today; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You have never investigated a murder, have you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that mean yes, you have, or yes, I'm right, you have not investigated a murder?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't conducted any murder investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In addition, moving now to the second topic that I want to cover, which is the way you went about preparing your report, in answer to some questions from Mr. Tapuskovic, you said it sounded like a little bit of frustration that you hadn't gotten to Sarajevo and seen these sites yourself? And that's true, isn't it? You didn't go to Sarajevo and look on the ground at these sites where these sniping incidents occurred, did you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not frustrated. I just stated that it would have been useful for photographs to be taken on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So it would have been useful but it is not something that you did in preparing your report. Fair statement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I just want to clear up one point about the report itself. At the beginning of your testimony, you said that the - and I may mispronounce this - the Dragunov weapon was not available at the time of these events. Is that -- am I remembering your testimony accurately?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was not in the arsenal of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, that is not the only weapon that fires a 7.62-millimetre round, is it? There are others.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about 7.62-millimetre calibre, it can be used by automatic rifles, Kalashnikov, and there is also PKT 7.62-millimetre, they are used by light machine-guns and machine-guns M-84. And the same calibre is used by M-76 sniper Dragunov.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And other than the last weapon you mentioned, the Dragunov, all of these weapons were available at the time of the events in question, that is, 1994, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in fact, in your own report, on page 10 of the English version and page 19 of the B/C/S version, you describe the 7.62-millimetre round as the most common weapon used in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about some of the specific events that Mr. Tapuskovic was questioning you on and I'm going to begin by talking about ranges, which is something you talked about at the -- in your testimony, and you'll remember we saw these pictures taken through a sight. Are you aware -- you testified about it being difficult to hit targets, and I think the farthest out you went was about 600 metres. Are you aware from reviewing Mr. Van der Weijden's report that the distance from the Metalka building to the tram tracks is 312 metres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to doubt that that's a reasonably accurate figure, 312 metres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked it on the map and on the internet and this distance is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It might be 310, it might be 320, but it's about that. Okay. And are you also aware that the distance from the school for the blind to the Vemeks department store or the victim of sniping 2 was shot is also about 250, 300 metres. Does that sound accurate to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also took this figure from Van der Weijden report who provided this measurement, so approximately it is 250 to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, the difference from Sharpstone down into Sedrenik is quite a bit longer. That's about a thousand metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several numbers, 900 to 1.200 metres, because it's a different position vis-a-vis Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Correct. And people are shot in different areas and so it varies. But between 900 and 1.200 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Mr. Weijden's report, and these measurements were also taken on the map, and this is the range within which they are stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And you are also aware that Mr. Van der Weijden, who is a sniper and has been one for some years, testified that there was not a difficulty in taking this shot from Sharpstone into Sedrenik. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of his testimony. I have studied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And although you are not a sniper, as a military officer, do you have any reason to quibble with the idea that a properly trained sniper can hit a target at ranges of between 900 and 1.200 metres, given the proper equipment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right when you say that it is conditional for him to have proper gear. The rifle that we are talking about, that is, an M-76 sniper rifle, does not have these features and due to that I provided photographs, because its optical sight allows for zooming in. To put it simply, the sight can magnify the view four times and that's a constant value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, but something needs to be changed and modified in the English version of what was said. At line 24, "because its optical sight allows for zooming in," it's the opposite that was said in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does not allow for zooming in. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you are aware that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You're aware both from your own military career and from Mr. Van der Weijden's report that snipers usually operate in teams; snipers generally do not work alone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule snipers around the world in general and in the JNA in particular are supposed to operate in pairs. But as per establishment, this is not envisaged as a given. It's just an optional category.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. There has been a document introduced in this trial - it is -- well, I'll get it in just a moment - but ordering certain individuals to go to sniper school and it's got General Milosevic's name on it as the person giving the order. The training in the JNA would have been for snipers to operate in these sniper/spotter pairs; is that correct? That is the preferred way for snipers to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, and I'm talking, Mr. President, about Exhibit P684.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was submitted to me and what my learned friend Mr. Docherty mentioned, that they operate in pairs, I wasn't able to see any such statement in any of the documents. I would like this document to be shown to the witness. There was mention of training but there was no mention of training them to operate in pairs. I wasn't able to see that anywhere and I would like this to be shown to the witness. Maybe it is an omission on my part, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, is this set out in the document --.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to which we referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No. And I never thought that it was. It's a document that says, Take these people and send them to sniper school. And now my question is, since the man has been in the JNA and the Serbian army for some years, what do they learn in sniper school? And I think the answer is they learn to operate in pairs but we'll see what the witness says. But no, it's not in the document. The document just says, Go to sniper school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. So we've got this document, Exhibit P684, that says the following named people are to go to sniper school, and my question is: From your experience in the Serbian army and the Yugoslavian People's Army, at sniper school aren't people taught to work in pairs, a sniper/spotter team?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the JNA rules, the training was conducted in such a way to train snipers to operate individually. Sometime after the 1990s when I was transferred or when I joined the Serbian army, or rather, the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I studied some foreign experiences and on the basis of that we introduced the training of snipers to operate in pairs. Before that the JNA only trained them to operate individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that change occurred, you said, during the -- was it the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mid-1990s, and I'm talking about the time when I was in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. So before or after the events that we're talking about in this case this morning?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. The sight that you were talking about was a mechanical sight that does not magnify, but there are also sights available to do magnify, aren't there? Two times, four times, and even higher numbers; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Another factor that would affect a sniper, and you talked about this, is the weather, and you talked about looking at the NATO weather reports. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And those weather reports are in evidence as Defence Exhibit 362.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we just take a look at them just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what I'm going to be asking you about, sir, is there is a column on these weather reports marked "visibility" and I'm going to ask you to take a look at those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could we move forward two or three pages and get to a page that's got some numbers on it. It would be a grid. That one will do fine. And then if we can zoom it up a bit so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you see, sir, the - I'm going to count, one, two, three, four, five, six - the seventh set of numbers? The top one there says 2.000. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that the visibility in metres?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only received a translation of this table and the only translation I have is just "visibility" or "poor visibility." I cannot comment, therefore, on the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And again -- well, I put it to you that these numbers never drop below 2.000. I mean, I don't want to take the time to look at every page of the report. But if those numbers do not drop below 2.000, then -- and the longest shot here is the Sharpstone-to-Sedrenik shot, that would mean the visibility throughout is always greater than the longest shot at issue. That was sort of a complicated question, but do you understand what I'm asking and can you answer it? Let me try again. The longest shot that we've been talking about is one of 1.200 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The lowest value for visibility in the NATO weather reports is 2.000 metres. And we can take the time and go through every page if we want to or you can accept my representation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to comment on what you said because these figures as shown in the terms that they are stated in are not clear to me and therefore I cannot make any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Well, this document is in evidence and we can perhaps direct attention to a page in which these -- in which these numbers are listed, and while that's being looked at we'll continue. You talked a bit about determining origin of fire, where a shot came from, and you remember you started off talking about how in an urban environment, because of the echoes and the reverberations, it can be difficult to tell the origin of fire. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And before I move on, we now have a page, do you see it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This is in English, but I saw from your curriculum vitae that you had at least some English language training in the army. And do you see that the column I've been referring to is "VSBY" and then in parentheses "metres"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a language course in the army. I paid for it myself. But I haven't had an opportunity to complete it, so I kindly ask you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. The misunderstanding was mine. But in any event the column is headed in a way that appears to be the English word "visibility" and the measurement is "metres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
