utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this interpretation offered by the Prosecution does not exist in the document. What the Prosecutor is saying is not in the document. There is not an expanded abbreviation anywhere in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you point us to what you've just said, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All I'm saying is the column, counting from the left, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It says "VSBY" and then "M" in brackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'm putting it to the witness that given the numbers here and that is a weather report, the most sensible interpretation is that that is the visibility measured in metres, and the witness can say yes or can say no. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Tapuskovic? You haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have seen it, Your Honours, and this does not mean what is being said. That's not what is written anywhere in the legend, what my learned friend Mr. Docherty is talking about, that it's the distance. These are the things in this document, because this document refers to the conditions prevailing at the airport that have to be very accurate, whereas the incident happened in close proximity of the airport. For that reason we used this document to check the visibility, and as it is stated in the introductory part of this document, we would be able to find out whether it was foggy or cloudy and we use these terms that were explicitly used in the document. We didn't offer any other interpretations apart from where it is being explicitly said that the weather was sunny, that it was cloudy or foggy. That's what we used without inputting any of our assessments or interpretations, apart from these basic data, such as fog, sunny weather or cloudy weather, as it is written in the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the point. Witness, do you agree with counsel's proposition that, given the numbers set out in that column, that this is a weather report and it is a measurement of the visibility in metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not clear to me and therefore I cannot say either yes or no because I don't know what I would be talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Going back, then, to echoes and reverberations, all of the items of analysis that you use in trying to determine origin of fire have their limitations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. All of them tell you some things but don't tell you some other things; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in working out origin of fire, isn't it true that you've got to use all of the information at your disposal, being aware of what it can and cannot tell you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was precisely analysing the available documentation from different angles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And in fact you testified a fair amount about angles and in particular about the path that bullets take through human bodies; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only mentioned the path that goes through a human body, but I didn't base my analysis on what happened in the section of that path. I only observed it as an integral part of a trajectory of a bullet passing through a human body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I understood it that way. And one of the reasons you didn't analyse it was because, as you testified, in many cases it wasn't there to be analysed, was it? It wasn't among the documentation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And you noted that absence and let's talk for a few minutes about what exactly is absent when this, as you called it, canal is not documented. First of all, you need to know very precisely the position of the person when the bullet struck them, don't you, in order for this canal to give you useful information about origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. If I turn slightly to the right or slightly to the left, we're going to get different answers, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Or if I bend over even just a little bit, we're going to get a different answer, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When bullets hit things, they often deflect, don't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the place of impact. However, the trajectory is not a straight line in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in fact the report that you read about sniping incident 2, the shot through the tunnel, indicated that the victim had been shot, I believe, in the shoulder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Shoulders have bones in them, don't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If a bullet hits a bone, then this canal through the body is not going to give you much useful information, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it hits a hard surface --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are back in the situation in which this witness is asked to tell us about things that only a physician could, an expert. I did not examine him on anything that had to do with the medical science. I didn't examine him on anything that falls within the scope of a medical expert. Now the witness is being asked to explain the behaviour of a bullet when hitting shoulder bones. This is completely beyond the scope of testimony of this witness and I ask you not to allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, the witness presents himself - excuse me - presents by the Defence as an expert in ballistics, in the behaviour of bullets, and I can change the question to ask what happens when bullets hit things that are hard and rely on everyone's common sense to know that bones are hard, if that would satisfy Mr. Tapuskovic. But I'm simply -- he testified about the canal through the body on his direct examination and I think I'm entitled to cross-examine about the limits of the information that we can learn from looking at the canal through the body made by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm afraid you opened the witness up to that kind of examination by leading evidence about the canal, and I'm going to allow the question but as reformulated by you, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So I'll put the question again as reformulated. When bullets hit things that are hard, their trajectory often changes; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if the bullets point -- if the bullet is deflected by hitting something hard, then the canal through the body is going to not give you accurate information about origin of fire, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that since it concerns the behaviour of a projectile through the body. I am not competent to testify on that part of trajectory. I am interested in the position of the entry and exit location. As to what happens in between, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So you're interested in the position of the entry and the exit. You're aware that sometimes between the entry and the exit, if the bullet hits something hard which we won't call a bone, it's going to change its trajectory, and you must be aware that if the trajectory changes, you're not going to be able to draw a straight line back to the origin of fire, aren't you, Colonel? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In addition to using all the different bits and pieces of information that are available and in addition to knowing the limitations of each bit of information, it's important when determining origin of fire also to use your common sense, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so when we're talking about determining origin of fire, some of the things you might be interested in knowing are where are the confrontation lines between the two opposing armies. That could be useful to your analysis, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case we have to know where the separation lines are between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You need to know which buildings have got -- have been documented as having sniping positions in them, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we, to take a concrete example, could please see e-court 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're still in the process of establishing that. It has not been established, the thing referred to by Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's that? Be more explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The place from which there was firing, the firing position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What Mr. Docherty asked is whether in any case it's necessary to know where the separation lines are between the two sides, and the witness answered, "You need to know which buildings --" oh, that's the -- this is the question. The question is: "You need to know which buildings have got -- what buildings have sniping positions in them," and the answer is yes. And your point is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can the witness deal with that? By what means? Other than -- well, I don't want to lead. But in general how can this witness respond to such a question? That question is difficult to understand. Perhaps it can be reformulated. How can the witness tell us anything about the location of firing positions and which buildings housed such positions, so that that would be a useful piece of information for us to be able to establish anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I haven't asked him to tell us which -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's an example that's being given. I don't see any problem with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Perhaps the question wasn't clear, so let me make it more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If a Canadian and a French officer saw in a particular building a position that looked to them as though it had been used for sniping, that is, it had sandbags, it had little holes cut in the wall for rifles, if you're trying to work out origin of fire, wouldn't you want to know where that building was? Isn't that one of the bits of information you'd like to have?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the example of a Canadian or French soldier observing, but I don't understand the thrust of your question. I cannot provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's try one last time and then we'll give up and move on. We're talking about the things that are useful to know when you're trying to work out where the shooter was who just shot this person who is lying in the street, okay? And I'm putting it to you: If one of the things, one of the bits of information that's out there is the documented existence of a sniper's position in a building, is that something you'd like to know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were given a document, but I don't have such a thing. You mentioned sandbags. There are things to camouflage one's position, but it doesn't necessarily mean that that particular place used to be a sniper position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe these are matters that are to be contemplated by the Bench itself and not by this witness. It includes certain facts that have not been ascertained yet and this witness cannot provide us with any useful information on that. This area falls within your remit once you set about deciding on the matters at hand. What we have here is an assertion of the existence of a position from which there was firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was put on a hypothetical basis and the witness has answered. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we see court exhibit 10, e-court page number 3, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, sir, is a photograph. It's a closer view of one that you were looking at on direct examination. Do you know which building in that photograph is the school for the blind?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this photograph it is the one with the slanted roof. That's the house for the blind, the school for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In working out your origin of fire on this sniping incident number 2, would it matter to you that on the side of that building that we're looking at in this photograph there are patched holes suitable for putting a rifle through; one at the very top and one, one floor down?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assumptions. I didn't see that and I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If there is evidence in this case to that effect, or - change the question - assume for purposes of this question, assume that these holes exist. Useful information in working out origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it is still an assumption. We are dealing here with exact facts. I do not wish to make use of any assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I know you don't wish to make use of them and I know you wouldn't ever do this professionally, make an assumption. But I'm asking you for purposes of this proceeding to make the assumption and tell us whether the existence of such holes would be useful to you in determining origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the position and the situation underneath the roof, whether anyone can actually position themselves below the roof, and I don't know what the exact height is, what the height of the wall is. Therefore, I do not have a specific answer for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, let's try something else. And this relates to shooting trams in the S curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, for purposes of the record, I'm going to be referring to testimony from a Defence witness at transcript pages 7273 and 7274 -- 7.273 and 7.274.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In working out origin of fire, would it be important for you to know that a Defence witness has testified that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had 12-man sniper units in high-rise buildings in the Grbavica area of Sarajevo? I mean, when you're trying to work out origin of fire, would it help you to know that there are actually snipers in buildings that have a line of sight onto the place where the person or the tram was shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can one ask such a question, and who can answer such a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a perfectly ordinary question in a proceeding of this kind. There's nothing wrong with it at all. It's the kind of question that is to be asked. If the witness can't answer it, then he can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, sir, or do you want me to ask it again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat it and try to make it shorter, since it contained a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'll do my best. I'll break it down into several questions. If a Defence witness has testified and that witness has knowledge of the location of snipers, would you want to know what those locations were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know such a witness. Oh, I guess you're asking me whether I would be interested in knowing what the locations are?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am still missing the thrust of your question. I don't know why you're asking me whether I would like to know the locations of the sniping positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me back up a little bit and then we'll move on one way or another. You're trying to work out where the gunman was who shot a tram in the S curve, okay? Take that as the starting point. Then take the further step that there's a witness who will say there were sniper teams in high-rise buildings with a line of sight to where the tram was shot, okay? Now, you've testified that it's important to use your common sense when doing an origin-of-fire analysis. Do you remember saying that? Okay. So do you want to know where the snipers are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the Defence case there were no witnesses who confirmed that he saw any sniping positions. There is no such a witness who was able to see what is now being put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm just looking for the citation, Your Honour. I had it a moment ago. I am referring to the testimony of Defence witness Radomir Visnjic. The transcript cite is page 7273 and transcript page 7274. On cross-examination this witness testified that he observed 12-man sniping teams with scoped rifles going into high-rise buildings in Grbavica. That's the basis for the question. I submit that it gives me a good-faith basis for asking the witness the question I just put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does. We're going to take the break. You can have a look, Mr. Tapuskovic, at the citation given during the break. And I have to say I don't understand the objections you have been making. In cross-examination it is quite natural for the cross-examiner to put questions on the basis either of his case or the case of the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour. But if anyone is being quoted, we should be given the reference. There was never a witness who said that there was a street-car being fired upon and this is what is now being put to the witness. Anything can be put to a witness, but it has to have been told by someone else. That witness never said he saw any street-cars being fired upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the issue really is whether the knowledge of the position of a sniper is a relevant factor to be taken into account. That is what -- that is the issue. We'll take the break and get back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Colonel, and then we'll be finished. You testified about the S curve in the tram line and about what could be -- from where that S curve could be seen. Do you remember that with Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, trams move slowly in the S curve; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But trams will also move slowly as they are slowing down to enter the S curve, won't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And would you also suppose that as a tram is leaving the S curve it takes some distance to accelerate and pick up speed again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So the area over which the tram is moving slowly is greater than just the S curve itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Over a range of 312 metres it is not possible to mistake a tram for any kind of legitimate military target, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the tram is clearly visible, then yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if some sort of horrible mistake was made and that horrible mistake was widely publicised, and by "horrible mistake" I mean a tram is mistaken for a military target and shot, one would not expect the horrible mistake to be made again, would one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. You don't need to answer that. I think that's speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You indicated that you have read Mr. Van der Weijden's report quite carefully, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You therefore know that in each of the 12 specific incidents discussed in Mr. Van der Weijden's report, Mr. Van der Weijden found that in no case should the shot have been taken because it was not possible to classify the target as military. Do you remember that conclusion to each of the incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one opinion in the form of an assumption and then we have an expert opinion and now we're looking for another expert opinion from this witness. Now he's supposed to give his opinion on another expert's opinion concerning the matter, referring to the most important facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think a substantial question has yet been asked. What's the question that you're going to pose?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to then have the witness affirm that in his report he did not contradict Mr. Van der Weijden on this point. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mean to dispute or confirm Mr. Van der Weijden's analysis. I only studied his analysis somewhat. I am a ballistics expert. And as for the other thing, it is an assumption. I am a ballistics expert and I have no answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You are aware through your military career of when it is that soldiers may legitimately open fire on a target; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I didn't understand it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You are aware from your military career that there are rules about when soldiers may legitimately open fire on a target; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You saw in Mr. Van der Weijden's report his conclusion that each and every one of these shots was illegitimate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was his conclusion. I studied it and I don't wish to provide any comments on Mr. Van der Weijden's analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from that I take it that I am correct that nowhere in your report do you contradict Mr. Van der Weijden's conclusion on that point?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards that, I did not contest it, nor did I dwell on those assertions any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: With that, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have but a few questions. First of all, since I omitted to do that, I'd like us to look at an MFI document, 3 -- D360, or rather, I'd like to have that admitted. That is the expert report which until now used to be MFI D360. Now it should be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document identified as D360 will now be admitted as D360.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamenov, in answering one of the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you did not visit the location of the individual incidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many years have you lived in Sarajevo and worked there as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo for 16 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by Mr. Docherty about whether you were frustrated or not, did you at a certain point really deem it necessary to go there and take photographs the way you did through the optical sight?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of my opinions and I put it forth to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I need to tell you what I told the witness when we discussed this. We would have tried to do that, but after the Court's visit to the location and given the conditions which we could not secure for us to be there safely, for example, at Spicaste Stijena or to get on top of the school for the blind or to go anywhere else from which it is alleged that there was firing, and it was simply not feasible for us. We could not risk it. We could not try to do anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I put that to you, Witness, as well.

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On one of Mr. Docherty's questions you said -- well, first of all, he asked you whether you were a sniper shooter and you also mentioned your sport activities as regards marksmanship. But tell us again, please, what is the basic task of you as a lecturer at the academy at which you used to teach? What were you tasked with conveying to your cadets and to your students?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the testimony I said that in addition to the theoretical part of the lecture, I also trained my cadets to use sidearms, rifles, and sniper rifles. We also carried out shooting exercises. And before they start shooting I demonstrate how to handle and shoot from a sniper rifle. I am well trained in handling one so that I could train my students.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you never conducted a murder investigation. However, as regards weapons, sniper rifles, trajectories, and everything you mentioned in the report, is there a secret of sorts that you would be unfamiliar with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this weaponry, in addition to the theoretical part which I teach to the students, I also do research. I test such weaponry just before they are put in operational use. Therefore, I had the opportunity to test the weapons mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the incident of firing from the school for the blind, were you ever told a piece of information by which it would be stated that the bullet which hit the victim hit any of the bones?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A bone in itself, what sort of an obstacle is it? Are there any other obstacles similar in nature to bones? What is the behaviour of a bullet hitting a bone or a similar surface?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot provide you with an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear counsel first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This is the very question that when I put to the witness Mr. Tapuskovic objected and was sustained on, so I object. It calls for medical expertise. Those were the grounds upon which Mr. Tapuskovic made the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you appear to be asking -- in fact, you are asking the witness what sort of obstacle does a bone constitute. Does that not require medical knowledge? The other question, Mr. Docherty, "What is the behaviour of a bullet hitting a bone or similar surface" may not require medical knowledge, but the first one would appear to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour, Judge Robinson, this was by way of introduction. What I'm interested in is the following: Once a bullet hits a bone or a hard surface, what is its behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the bullet hitting a bone, I'm not capable of giving you an answer. As for other obstacles, it depends on the hardness and the bullet may behave differently. It may pierce it, it may break into two, it may be stopped, so there are different outcomes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can it bounce off?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's what I said at the beginning when I was talking about ricochetting. It can even bounce back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. But I have to tell you that I'm feeling rather under the weather. I will try to continue. I have some stomach problems, but I will try and do my best to continue the proceedings. I will try to continue my work and I'm not going to stop for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you're ill, you're ill, and I would not pressure you to continue if you are ill. But that's a decision for you. Judge Harhoff has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would just like to revert to one specific answer you gave to a question, I believe it was by the Prosecution, in relation to fragmentation bullets. The reason I'm asking is that we have had in this case some indication of the possibility that fragmentation bullets could have been used. Now, in your answer to the question you said that with the weaponry, and I'm quoting from your testimony just a while ago, "with the weaponry used in these incidents" - and this is on page 31, line 12 - "these being sniping rifles, automatic rifles, and light machine-guns, there is no such bullet which would have the fragmentation effect. We only have the classical bullet; then we have a marker bullet, an armour bullet, and incendiary bullet, and this is all for the 7.62-millimetre calibre." That was your answer. My question, therefore, is: Would fragmentation bullets be applied in the conflict in Bosnia with other calibre weapons? Were there, in other words, other weapons in use during the conflict other than 7.62-millimetre calibre which could use fragmentation bullets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, there were none of these fragmentation bullet calibres in the arsenal, either for rifle or machine-guns. There were no fragmentation bullets in the arsenal of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand you to say that there were no weaponry that could shoot fragmentation bullets, not 7.62 nor any other weaponry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN STAMENOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Stamenov, and I thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you mentioned your health, that you are not feeling well, and I'm mindful of that, so it's really for you to determine whether you wish to continue. The Chamber is quite prepared to take account of that and we believe that we still have enough time to get through our work. The work of the Tribunal is, of course, of paramount importance but so is your health.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and this is precisely why I was thinking about this. I think I can hardly continue with full concentration and I would kindly ask you to allow us to continue tomorrow. I believe that we have enough time, especially since this next witness shouldn't take too long. We still have about 40 or 50 minutes, and if it is possible, I would kindly ask you to allow for an adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In light of the special circumstances and the representations made by Mr. Tapuskovic about his health, the Chamber determines that we'll break now and resume tomorrow in the hope that the time available to you will allow you to recover, Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
